 UV filters spotlight: Environmental impact and SPF testing methods
 Kacey Culliney (Photo: Rido / AdobeStock ©) 
 17 November 2026 
 Share: 
 Industry needs to take a multistakeholder approach to measuring the environmental impact of UV filters and continue to invest in new SPF testing methods and better consumer education, say experts.
 Addressing attendees at this year’s UK Cosmetic, Toiletry and Perfumery Association’s (CTPA) inaugural scientific conference, two sunscreen experts said scientific gaps must be plugged and advances followed to keep data and knowledge relevant and reliable.
 Public concern on sunscreens
 Carys Mitchelmore, professor at the University of Maryland Center for Environmental Science , said that public perception of sunscreens changed after the publication of one study by Downs et al. in 2016 examining the toxicity of the UV sunscreen filter oxybenzone on coral systems in Hawaii and the US Virgin Islands . “ Because of that paper, there was a lot of media and social media noise and legislative actions taken – there were sunscreen bans in Hawaii in 2018, for example, and bans in the US Virgin Islands and other places, ” Mitchelmore said.
 The concern from a scientific perspective, however, is that a lot of action and opinion was formed from just one individual study, she said.
 In the years since, efforts have been made to balance out that noise, she explained. In 2022, the US non-profit National Academies of Sciences, Engineering and Medicine (NASEM) published a consensus study report reviewing the fate, exposure and effects of sunscreens in aquatic environments – work Mitchelmore was involved in at committee level.
 Findings showed variation in the relevance and reliability of methods used in UV filter aquatic toxicity studies, with many lacking standard procedures or standard test species making it difficult to compare results. Many studies also only analysed exposure in very localised settings, with single-time samples, creating a lot of spatial and temporal variability. The review also identified a significant knowledge gap in data for the chronic toxicity of UV filters.
 “ There were two main recommendations from this study, ” Mitchelmore told attendees. “ The first is that the US Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) should conduct an ecological risk assessment for all currently marketed UV filters and any new ones that become available. The second is getting collaboration from different stakeholders–people from industry, academia, trade associations, NGOs–to work together and fund, support and share data. ”
 Hazard + Exposure + Terminology
 Critically, Mitchelmore said more needs to be done to assess the true toxicity and environmental risk of UV filters in aquatic environments via environmental risk assessments (ERAs) that consider both hazard (how toxic a compound is to an organism) and exposure (the level and concentration a chemical is found in the environment).
 “ A more toxic chemical is not necessarily the one that poses the greater environmental risk; it depends on toxicity, the hazard and actual environmental exposure, ” she explained. Concentration and whether a chemical is absorbed by an organism, therefore, needs to be put in context; simple detection of a chemical does not directly mean harm.
 The professor said misrepresentation of chemical pollutants and UV filters in the media also needs to be addressed. UV filters are often grouped together, she said, yet they are “ incredibly different from eachother ”, with different chemical profiles and physical properties. Terms are also widely misused when describing chemicals, particularly the word ’toxin’, she said. “ I see ’toxin’ used all the time for synthetic chemicals but a toxin is, specifically, a poisonous substance produced by a biological organism. ’Toxicant’ is okay if it is a chemical capable of causing adverse effect; ’contaminant’ is a chemical present but it doesn’t imply toxicity or risk. ”
 Marc Pissavini, sun research lab director at Coty , said the misuse of language around UV filters and chemicals also relates to human health. “ We have seen lots of fake news and dangerous chemical headlines, ” Pissavini said, with misinformation stretching even further today on social media platforms like TikTok.
 Much of this messaging promotes sunscreen avoidance which is especially worrying given that around eight million people worldwide are diagnosed with skin cancer each year due to over-exposure, he said.
 From an industry perspective, there is a real responsibility to not only educate consumers on the importance of sun protection but also make the whole process simpler and more accessible, Pissavini said.
 Currently, the Sun Protection Factor (SPF) system used on suncare products is poorly understood by consumers , the professor said, and testing conditions do not representative real-use, which depends on various paramenters, including skin phototype, spreadability, the location and environment in which the product is used. “ It’s very, very complicated, ” he said, “ ...it’s difficult to say that 30 SPF is higher protection than 15 SPF in real life. ” This, he said, makes it complex to communicate to consumers.
 Regulatory updates: ISO methods and EU recommendations
 Recent updates at international and EU level should help advance and improve SPF communication, Pissavini said.
 In December 2024, the International Organization for Standardization (ISO) introduced two new in vitro methods for assessing the SPF of sunscreen products : ISO 23675:2024 and ISO 23698:2024 .
 ISO 23675:2024 , also known as the Double Plate Method (DPM), uses robotics and plates to spread product. ISO 23698:2024 , also known as the Hybrid Diffuse Reflectance Spectroscopy (HDRS) method, conducts an optical assessment of sunscreen products in a non-invasive way. Both methods are standardised, repeatable, reproducible, cost-effective and fast, Pissavini said.
 At EU level, the European Commission is also finalising its revision of the 2006 EU Sunscreen Recommendation (2006/647/EC) which should be published in the first-quarter of 2027. Crucially, the professor said this revision will cover all products making SPF claims, which is “ a major change ” for the industry. Up until now, SPF claims have been split into primary and secondary: primary meaning SPF is the primary product claim (sunscreen products) and secondary meaning SPF is a secondary claim (moisturisers with SPF).
 In addition to this, SPF 10 will no longer be authorised in primary SPF products and there will be a new claim on “ enhanced UVA protection ”, though a clear definition is yet to be finalised, he said.
 Looking ahead, Mitchelmore said that any policy or management actions taken in the sunscreen and UV filter space will require consideration of both human and ecological outcomes, and coordination across multiple agencies and organisations. “ The key thing is we need transparency, open-access data, communication–especially to the public–and collaboration between all stakeholders, ” she concluded.
